L0@P0: The Learning with Errors Problem
L1@P0: Oded Regev∗
L2@P0: Abstract
L3@P0: In this survey we describe the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem, discuss its properties,
L4@P0: its hardness, and its cryptographic applications.
L5@P0: 1 Introduction
L6@P0: In recent years, the Learning with Errors (LWE) problem, introduced in [Reg05], has turned out to
L7@P0: be an amazingly versatile basis for cryptographic constructions. Its main claim to fame is being as
L8@P0: hard as worst-case lattice problems, hence rendering all cryptographic constructions based on it
L9@P0: secure under the assumption that worst-case lattice problems are hard. Our goal in this survey is
L10@P0: to present the state-of-the-art in our understanding of this problem. Although all results presented
L11@P0: here already appear in the literature (except for the observation in Appendix A), we tried to make
L12@P0: our presentation somewhat simpler than that in the original papers. For more information on
L13@P0: LWE and related problems, see some of the recent surveys on lattice-based cryptography [MR08,
L14@P0: Pei09b, Mic07, Reg06].

L91@P2: problem. This is closely related to the fact that the best known algorithms for lattice problems [AKS01,

L93@P2: Hardness. There are several reasons to believe the LWE problem is hard. First, because the best
L94@P2: known algorithms for LWE run in exponential time (and even quantum algorithms don’t seem to
L95@P2: help). Second, because it is a natural extension of the LPN problem, which is itself an extensively
L96@P2: studied problem in learning theory that is widely believed to be hard. Moreover, LPN can be
L97@P2: formulated as the problem of decoding from random linear binary codes, hence any algorithmic
L98@P2: progress on LPN is likely to lead to a breakthrough in coding theory.
L99@P2: Third, and most importantly, because LWE is known to be hard based on certain assumptions regarding the worst-case hardness of standard lattice problems such as GAPSVP (the decision version of the shortest vector problem) and SIVP (the shortest independent vectors problem) [Reg05, Pei09a]. More precisely, when the modulus q is exponential, hardness is based on
L100@P2: the standard assumption that GAPSVP is hard to approximate to within polynomial factors. For
L101@P2: polynomial moduli q (which is the more interesting setting for cryptographic applications), the
L102@P2-3: 3hardness is based on slightly less standard (but still quite believable) assumptions. Namely, either that GAPSVP is hard to approximate even given a ‘hint’ in the form of a short basis, or that
L103@P3: GAPSVP or SIVP are hard to approximate to within polynomial factors even with a quantum
L104@P3: computer.
L105@P3: We note that SIVP is in some sense harder than GAPSVP, and the fact that we have hardness
L106@P3: based on SIVP is crucial for establishing the hardness of the ring-LWE problem described below.
L107@P3: We also note that the above results require q to be somewhat large (typically, at least √
L108@P3: n) and
L109@P3: hence do not apply to LPN, i.e., the case q = 2. Finally, we remark that the approximation factors
L110@P3: obtained for the worst-case lattice problems are typically of the form O˜(n/α), explaining why we
L111@P3: prefer to have α ≥ 1/poly(n). A further discussion of the known hardness results will be given in
L112@P3: Section 2.
L113@P3: Thanks to these strong hardness results, a reader skeptical of the hardness of LWE can view
L114@P3: the work in this area as attempts to find (possibly quantum) algorithms for worst-case lattice

L31: ### 【17†A Decade of Lattice Cryptography】
L32: 
L33: Chris Peikert
L34: ##### Abstract
L35: \emph{Lattice-based cryptography} is the use of conjectured hard problems on point lattices in~$\R^{n}$ as the foundation for secure cryptographic systems. Attractive features of lattice cryptography include apparent resistance to \emph{quantum} attacks (in contrast with most number-theoretic cryptography), high asymptotic efficiency and parallelism, security under \emph{worst-case} intractability assumptions, and solutions to long-standing open problems in cryptography.
L36: This work surveys most of the major developments in lattice cryptography over the past ten years. The main focus is on the foundational \emph{short integer solution}~(SIS) and \emph{learning with errors}~(LWE) problems (and their more efficient ring-based variants), their provable hardness assuming the worst-case intractability of standard lattice problems, and their many cryptographic applications.
